clue.text: Woman in charge, a complainer, ruler in muddle

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one group of letters goes within another

parts.note: a muddle is a mess
taken as written
a nag is someone who complains persistently
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword's stock ruler

explanation.surface: A bossy woman is dismissed as a whinger, and the ruler is in a pickle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman in charge' is the definition, so the first 'in' belongs to it; the container signal is the later 'in' before 'muddle'. ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A manageress is the female form of manager, a woman who runs a shop, office or business.

clue.text: Nasty plan

definitions.meaning: a verb, to intend or have in mind

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a nasty scheme, but they are two separate meanings of one word, an adjective and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as an adjective for unkind behaviour and as a verb for having something in mind as an intention.

clue.text: Charming home set up overlooking church

indicators.note: in a down entry, to overlook is to sit above, so the first piece stands on top of the next
in a down clue, setting something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A charming house built on a hill above the parish church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' gives the word for being at home, as in 'staying in tonight'; CE, Church of England, is the standard crossword church.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice and charming are both everyday adjectives for someone or something pleasant and agreeable.

clue.text: Good to reduce the courage of potential killer

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
to unman someone is to sap their nerve

explanation.surface: Advice that it is a good idea to rattle the nerve of a would-be assassin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'good to' as 'it is good to', but G is simply the abbreviation placed before the verb for weakening resolve.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunman carries a firearm and so is someone who may kill, a would-be shooter or armed attacker.

clue.text: Try something that looks impossible? Oh, from earth once very tricky!

indicators.note: something tricky is devious and twisty, so the letters are twisted into another order

parts.note: the fifteen letters of these words, used as they stand

explanation.surface: Talk of an impossible venture, with a nostalgic sigh about when leaving earth once seemed wildly hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The earth and the moon in the surface nicely echo the answer's image, which helps confirm the rearrangement once a few letters are in.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means aiming very high, setting a goal that seems beyond reach, as the moon once was.

clue.text: Mum is upset — time to give things up?

indicators.note: to upset is to turn over, and in a down clue that flips the letters to read upward

parts.note: taken as written
Lent is the season when many Christians give up a luxury

explanation.surface: Mother is distressed: is it time to make sacrifices?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother but is the adjective meaning saying nothing, as in 'keep mum'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be mum is to stay quiet and keep a secret, so it matches an adjective for making no sound.

clue.text: Gardener's son revealed by Somerset House

indicators.note: what is revealed by some words is already there to be uncovered within them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A gardener's boy is exposed by the records at Somerset House, a London building once holding birth registers.
explanation.walkthrough: The gardener is Adam, who tended Eden; SETH was his third son in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam was put in the Garden of Eden to tend it, and Genesis names Seth as the son born after Abel's death.

clue.text: Chosen man in charge of modern type of technology

definitions.note: a noun phrase; the answer is the adjective describing that kind of technology

parts.note: the elect are those chosen
a man's name
IC is short for in charge

explanation.surface: A newly appointed manager put in charge of the latest tech department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In charge of' looks like one phrase, but IC takes only 'in charge' and 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Electronic devices, built on circuits and transistors, are the basis of most current technology, from phones to computers.

clue.text: When trained he's a better animal

indicators.note: training reshapes and reorders, so these letters are drilled into a new form

parts.note: the letters of these words, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A boast that a pet, once schooled, becomes a finer creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an uncommon word, so the checking letters matter.
explanation.definitionFit: The hartebeest is a large African antelope with long face and curved horns, so it is a kind of beast.

clue.text: A ben scaled could be construed as this

definitions.text: A ben scaled could be construed as this

indicators.note: to construe is to interpret, and a fresh interpretation lets the letters be read in another order

parts.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: A Scottish mountain that has been climbed must be one that can be climbed.
explanation.walkthrough: A ben is a Scottish mountain. The whole clue both supplies the letters and describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: If a peak has been scaled it has been proved climbable, which is what the adjective says.

clue.text: Wise guy, the crossword compiler — but not an abstainer

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes something, so part of the preceding word is left out

parts.note: a setter is the person who writes a crossword
TT, teetotal, marks someone who abstains from drink

explanation.surface: A smart-alec crossword writer who is fond of a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wise guy' sounds like a smart-alec, but here it means a sage; TT removed from SETTER leaves SEER.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer is a prophet or sage with insight into the future, so a wise man rather than a joker.

clue.text: Groups coming together chat about Wagner's work

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: to gas is to chatter idly
The Ring cycle is Wagner's four-opera masterpiece

explanation.surface: Societies meeting up to talk about a Wagner opera.
explanation.walkthrough: GAS splits round THE RING, Wagner's Ring of the Nibelung cycle.
explanation.definitionFit: Gatherings are assemblies or meetings of people who have come together in one place.

clue.text: Source established beyond doubt — one of the forebears half forgotten

indicators.note: to forget half of something is to drop half its letters

parts.note: something proven is shown to be true
a forebear is an ancestor

explanation.surface: An antique's origin authenticated, though one of its ancestors has partly slipped from memory.
explanation.walkthrough: Half forgotten means exactly half the letters go: the eight-letter word for a forebear keeps only its first four.
explanation.definitionFit: Provenance is the origin or documented history of something, especially an artwork, so its source.

clue.text: Hitting the sack with only a bit of the body tucked in

indicators.note: whatever is tucked in is pushed inside something else

parts.note: a sack is a bag
the shin is part of the leg

explanation.surface: Going to bed with barely any part of oneself under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hitting the sack' reads as the idiom for going to bed, but the definition is only 'Hitting' and 'the sack' is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bashing is striking hard, so it is a stronger synonym for hitting something or someone.

clue.text: Country vehicle conveying drunken earl

indicators.note: to convey is to carry, and a carrier holds its load inside

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rural bus taking home an intoxicated nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like an adjective for the vehicle; it is the definition, and BUS carries a rearranged EARL.
explanation.definitionFit: Belarus is an Eastern European nation bordered by Russia, Poland and Ukraine, so it is a sovereign state.

clue.text: Floral arrangement guy brought up and put down

indicators.note: bringing something up lifts it, so in this vertical entry its letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: to guy someone is to mock them, and so is to rag them
to land an aircraft is to put it down

explanation.surface: A florist lifts a display, then sets it down again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' reads as a man, but it is the verb meaning to tease; that verb, flipped, starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A garland is a wreath or ring of flowers and leaves, worn or hung as decoration.

clue.text: Chaps in planes mean to fly across Ireland

indicators.note: one thing spread across another straddles it, holding it in the middle
flying scatters things, so the letters are sent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
IR is an abbreviation for Ireland

explanation.surface: Pilots who intend to make a flight over Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean to fly' reads as intending a flight, but 'mean' is the letters and 'to fly' mixes them into AMEN around IR.
explanation.definitionFit: Airmen are aviators, especially members of an air force, so they are men who fly aircraft.

clue.text: Shabby-sounding item taken from Hamish's allotment?

indicators.note: what is sounding is heard, so the answer is the spoken form of a word

parts.note: tatty means worn and shabby

explanation.surface: A worn-looking vegetable dug up from a Scotsman's garden plot.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamish is a typically Scottish name, pointing to the Scots word for a potato; an allotment is a small rented vegetable plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattie is Scots for potato, a crop likely to be dug up from a Scottish gardener's vegetable plot.

clue.text: Be a bit mad, having lost the thread?

definitions.text: Be a bit mad, having lost the thread?

parts.note: surface reading: to be slightly crazy
setter's reading: a fastener whose spiral groove has stripped no longer holds tight

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost the thread' sounds like losing track of an argument, but a stripped thread is also what leaves a fixing loose in its hole.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone as eccentric or slightly crazy, pictured as a machine with a fixing come undone.

clue.text: Dismissed a knight involved in heavy defeat

indicators.note: whatever is involved in something is wrapped up inside it

parts.note: a rout is a crushing defeat
N is the chess notation for a knight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A knight who took part in a crushing loss has been sent away.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batter is run out when the fielders break the wicket before the batter reaches the crease.
explanation.definitionFit: Run out is one way a batter's innings is ended in cricket, so a batter who was run out was dismissed.

clue.text: Girl runs into river — start of adventure

indicators.note: to run into something is to enter it, so one letter goes inside

parts.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A girl dashes into a river, the beginning of an escapade.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tees flows through Middlesbrough to the North Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Teresa is a female given name, and crosswords use 'girl' to clue any woman's name.

clue.text: More than one animal goes by sea — any number brought aboard

indicators.note: whatever is brought aboard a vessel ends up inside it

parts.note: to sail is to travel by sea
N stands for any number in mathematics

explanation.surface: Several creatures travel on a ship, with any amount of them taken on board.
explanation.walkthrough: The Noah's Ark picture hides a slow-moving answer: N goes inside SAILS.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a plural, and each snail is a mollusc, so the phrase describes several creatures.

clue.text: Older one is falling apart, little right!

indicators.note: something falling apart loses its structure, so its letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
R is the short form of right

explanation.surface: An elderly person's body is failing, and they are rather indignant about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little right' tells you to use the abbreviation, not the full word.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior as an adjective means higher in age, used of the elder of two people with the same name.

clue.text: Leader of Democrats backing savage cut

indicators.note: to back something is to stand behind it, so this piece comes after the other

parts.note: savage and severe both mean harsh or brutal

indicators.note: the leader of a group is the one out in front, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: The head of the Democrats supports a brutal spending cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like a reversal, but here it means supporting from behind, so the letter simply follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Severed is a past tense and participle meaning chopped or sliced off, like a rope or a link cut through.

clue.text: Return of workers' organisation one dismissed as unacceptable to toffs

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the letters read from the end
whatever is dismissed is sent away, so it drops out of the word

parts.note: a trade union organises workers
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A trade union returns, and one member is sacked for being too common for the posh.
explanation.walkthrough: UNION flipped is NOINU; losing I gives NONU. U and non-U were 1950s labels for upper-class and not upper-class speech; a toff is a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-U describes words and habits not considered upper class, so posh people would frown upon them.

clue.text: Bit of the crust a light brown?

indicators.note: a bit of something is a portion lying within it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the second

explanation.surface: A piece of pastry crust might be pale golden.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that crust colour is only a suggestion; the answer sits across two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is the pale greyish-yellow or beige shade of unbleached linen, so a light brownish colour.

clue.text: Gee, boy is cock-a-hoop!

parts.note: gee is how the letter G is written out
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise that a boy is thrilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gee' looks like an exclamation of surprise but is the spelled-out name of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock-a-hoop means delighted or elated, so it is a livelier synonym for pleased and happy.

clue.text: A docile man stirred up, influenced by a devil

indicators.note: stirring mixes contents around, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A meek man is roused to fury, as if under a demon's sway.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's docile man turned wild neatly suits an answer about possession.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoniacal describes someone possessed by a demon, or acting as though a fiend controlled them.

clue.text: Vehicle was first after starting second

indicators.note: something coming after a starter is placed behind it, so the order is fixed

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
whoever was first in a race led it

explanation.surface: A car that was leading after starting in second place.
explanation.walkthrough: The racing picture of a car moving up from second hides a winter conveyance.
explanation.definitionFit: A sled is a vehicle on runners for travel over snow or ice, pulled by dogs or people.

clue.text: Mob around Italy getting about, making advance

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a mob is a gang
I is the international vehicle code for Italy
about and round both mean approximately or in the vicinity

explanation.surface: A crowd moving about Italy, pushing forward.
explanation.walkthrough: I is Italy's international vehicle registration code, as seen on car stickers.
explanation.definitionFit: To gain ground is an idiom for making progress or moving forward, taken from armies taking territory.
